newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: G10 recommends RTGS to reduce systemic risks.
newsitem.headline: G10 recommends RTGS to reduce systemic risks.

text.p: Real-time gross settlement (RTGS) systems offer a powerful method for reducing settlement and systemic risks in the world's interbank transfer systems, which daily processes in excess of $5.0 trillion, the Group of 10 (G10) leading industrial nations said on Monday.

In an effort to educate financial markets about the benefits of RTGS systems, G10 central banks released an overview of how various systems function and concluded there is no unique solution, but what works best for a particular country depends on its specific circumstances.

The report -- Real-time Gross Settlement Systems -- was prepared by G10's Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS), which is charged with improving the infrastracture that underpin financial markets, essentially the plumbing network that links the worlds' economies.

The report, which did not make specific recommendations for a specific type of RTGS system, was issued under the aegis of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), central bank to the worlds' central banks.

Most recently CPSS and its chairman New York Federal Reserve president William McDonough launched a strategy to reduce the risks of a breakdown in foreign exchange settlement systems, which account for a major share of large-value payment systems.

Large-value payment systems differ from retail fund transfer systems -- which for example handle cheques -- not only in the average size of transfers, but in the time sensitivity because they are used to settle financial market transactions.
The CPSS report comes amidst efforts by commercial bankers to develop a global clearing house for foreign exchange deals that connects national payment systems based on RTGS.

The work by the Group of 20 (G20), which comprises some of the world's largest players in the foreign exchange market, is based on the principle of Continuous Linked Settlements (CLS) and the efforts are encouraged by central bankers,

Payment and settlement systems are essential to the smooth functioning of financial markets and economies, but central bankers worry that many of the current systems expose banks to substantial interbank risks.

The nightmare that haunts central bankers is that the failure of one bank could lead to the failure of other banks due to these interbank exposures. This could trigger a systemic risk to the worldwide financial system.
"By their very nature networks, interbank payment and settlement systems are potentially a key institutional channel for the propagation of systemic crises," the report said.
Because of such concerns, many countries have made their payment systems more robust and mainly turned to RTGS systems.
An RTGS system processes and settles payment instructions between banks individually and continously throughout the day.

This contrasts with the traditional paper-based clearing houses and the more modern electronic equivalents where payment instructions are processed thoughout the day, but settlement among banks with central bank money first takes place later, typically at the end of the day.

This time lag between initiation of payment messages and final settlement is a major source of settlement risk because the bank sending an instruction could fail or not be able to settle obligations when due.

"The attraction of RTGS systems is that payee banks and their customers receive funds with certainty, or so-called finality, during the day, enabling them to use the funds immediately without exposing themselves to risks," it said.
To the extent sufficient funds are available at the time of processing in an RTGS system, the settlement lags approach zero, eliminating the primary risk in interbank transfers.

Most G10 countries already have RTGS systems in place, or are planning to introduce them soon. European Union (EU) central banks have decided all members should have RTGS systems so they can be linked together in TARGET, a pan-European system.
G10 consists of 11 countries: the United States, Japan, Germany, Canada, Britain, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Switzerland.
